trite

TRYT -- one syllable, rhymes with 'bright.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Trite is overused and lacking originality.

Movie critics groaned at the film's trite ending, in which the hero wakes to find it was all a dream.

Example

The new greeting-card writer drafts her first birthday line: 'Reach for the stars!' Her supervisor slides over a binder of cards from the last thirty years -- the trite phrase appears in more than two hundred of them.

Trite means overused and lacking originality. The word is aimed at language and ideas -- phrases, sayings, plot devices -- that once had force but have been repeated so many times they now land with no impact at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

worn-out: Worn-out applies to anything drained of usefulness by use -- worn-out shoes, a worn-out excuse, a worn-out worker. Trite is the word for expressions and ideas specifically: language repeated until it lands with no impact. A sweater can be worn-out; only words and ideas are trite.

corny: Corny means so cheesy and overly sentimental that it makes an audience groan -- a corny pun, a corny love scene. A trite phrase draws groans for a different reason: not gooey feeling, but sheer overuse. Corny fails by being mushy; trite fails by being worn flat from repetition.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fresh: new and original

original: invented newly, not copied

Where it sits · how worn out the expression is — stale → trite → hackneyed

stale vs. trite: Stale says the joke or phrase has simply lost its freshness, while trite adds a judgment: the expression was reached for lazily, because everyone always reaches for it.

hackneyed vs. trite: Hackneyed is the strongest of the three: a trite line makes readers sigh, but a hackneyed one has been worked so hard for so long that critics treat using it as a small offense.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Trite comes straight from Latin tritus, 'rubbed away' -- the past participle of terere, 'to rub, to wear down.' A trite phrase is literally a worn one: handled so many times, like an old coin rubbed smooth, that its face has disappeared.

Use the root in a new word: attrition

Use the root in a new word: attrition: The quarterly report devotes an entire page to attrition.

Root Check

Word Choice

Trite targets expressions and ideas: a trite phrase, trite dialogue, a trite moral, a trite plot twist. Keep it apart from its unit-mate banal -- banal covers broader dullness (a banal building, banal small talk), while trite specifically accuses language of being worn out through repetition. If it isn't words or an idea, banal is probably the better word.
